notes:
Conductance

  • Conductivity $\kappa = \dfrac{1}{\rho}$; molar conductivity $\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa\times1000}{C}$ (C in mol L$^{-1}$; $\Lambda_m$ in S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$).
  • For weak electrolytes $\Lambda_m$ increases sharply on dilution (more dissociation); for strong electrolytes it increases slightly (Debye-Hückel-Onsager, less ionic interaction). Degree of dissociation $\alpha = \Lambda_m/\Lambda_m^\circ$ (for weak electrolytes).
  • Kohlrausch's law of independent migration: $\Lambda_m^\circ = \lambda^\circ_+ + \lambda^\circ_-$ (used to find $\Lambda_m^\circ$ of weak electrolytes from strong electrolyte data).

Electrochemical Cells

  • Galvanic (voltaic) cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy ($\Delta G < 0$); electrolytic cell converts electrical to chemical energy ($\Delta G > 0$, non-spontaneous).
  • Anode = oxidation (in a galvanic cell, negative terminal); Cathode = reduction (positive terminal). In electrolysis, anode is positive, cathode is negative.
  • Cell notation: Zn(s)|Zn$^{2+}$(aq)||Cu$^{2+}$(aq)|Cu(s); anode written left, cathode right, salt bridge = ||.
  • $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$; cell reaction spontaneous if $E^\circ_{cell} > 0$, i.e. $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{cell} < 0$.

Nernst Equation

  • $E_{cell} = E^\circ_{cell} - \dfrac{2.303RT}{nF}\log Q$; at 298 K, $\dfrac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.0591$ V, so $E_{cell} = E^\circ_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n}\log Q$.
  • At equilibrium $E_{cell} = 0$: $\log K_c = \dfrac{nE^\circ_{cell}}{0.0591}$.
  • $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{cell} = -RT\ln K_c$.

Electrolysis & Faraday's Laws

  • 1st law: $w = Zit$ where $Z$ = electrochemical equivalent, $i$ = current (A), $t$ = time (s). 1 Faraday = 96500 C mol$^{-1}$ = charge of 1 mole electrons.
  • $w = \dfrac{M\times i\times t}{n\times96500}$ (M = molar mass, n = electrons transferred per ion).
  • 2nd law: same charge through different electrolytes deposits masses proportional to their equivalent weights.

Batteries, Fuel Cells & Corrosion

CellTypeKey point
Dry (Leclanché)PrimaryZn anode, graphite/MnO$_2$ cathode, ~1.5 V, non-rechargeable
Lead storageSecondaryPb anode, PbO$_2$ cathode, H$_2$SO$_4$; rechargeable, ~2 V/cell
H$_2$-O$_2$ fuel cell-H$_2$/O$_2$ over Pt electrodes with KOH; product only H$_2$O; pollution-free, high efficiency
  • Corrosion (rusting of iron) is an electrochemical process: Fe oxidised at anodic spot, O$_2$ reduced at cathodic spot in moist air, forming hydrated Fe$_2$O$_3$. Prevented by galvanising, painting, alloying, sacrificial protection (Zn/Mg block, more reactive than Fe).

Exam tip

KCET usually asks 3-4 questions from Electrochemistry: expect a Nernst equation numerical, a Faraday's law (electrolysis) numerical, one on conductance/Kohlrausch, and one conceptual (cell notation, galvanic vs electrolytic, or corrosion/battery facts).

questions.q: In the galvanic cell Zn(s)|Zn$^{2+}$(aq)||Cu$^{2+}$(aq)|Cu(s), the cathode is
questions.explanation: By convention the cathode is written on the right; reduction (Cu$^{2+}$ + 2e$^-$ $\to$ Cu) occurs there, while oxidation of Zn occurs at the anode on the left.
questions.trick: Cathode = right side of cell notation = reduction always.

questions.q: Given $E^\circ_{Cu^{2+}/Cu} = 0.34$ V and $E^\circ_{Zn^{2+}/Zn} = -0.76$ V, the standard EMF of the Daniell cell is
questions.explanation: $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10$ V (Cu is cathode, Zn is anode).
questions.trick: $E^\circ_{cell}=E^\circ_{cathode}-E^\circ_{anode}$ (right minus left).

questions.q: For the cell reaction $Zn + Cu^{2+} \to Zn^{2+} + Cu$ with $E^\circ_{cell} = 1.10$ V, $\Delta G^\circ$ is (F = 96500 C mol$^{-1}$, n = 2)
questions.explanation: $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{cell} = -2\times96500\times1.10 = -212300$ J mol$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: $\Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ_{cell}$ — plug n, F, E directly.

questions.q: A current of 2 A is passed for 965 seconds through molten NaCl. The mass of Na deposited is (Na = 23, F = 96500 C)
questions.explanation: Charge $= it = 2\times965 = 1930$ C $= 0.02$ F. Na$^+$ + e$^-$ $\to$ Na needs 1 F per mole, so mass $= 0.02\times23 = 0.46$ g.
questions.trick: $w=\dfrac{it}{F}\times M$ (n=1 for Na$^+$) — Faraday's first law.

questions.q: The same quantity of electricity is passed through separate cells of AgNO$_3$ and CuSO$_4$ solutions. If 5.4 g of Ag (M = 108) is deposited, the mass of Cu (M = 63.5) deposited is
questions.explanation: Moles of electrons $= 5.4/108 = 0.05$ mol e$^-$. Cu$^{2+}$ needs 2 e$^-$ per atom, so moles Cu $= 0.05/2 = 0.025$; mass $= 0.025\times63.5 = 1.588$ g.
questions.trick: Same charge → equal moles of e⁻; use $n_e=w/M$ then scale by valency.

questions.q: For a weak electrolyte, molar conductivity increases sharply with dilution mainly because
options: the degree of dissociation increases, producing more ions
questions.explanation: Weak electrolytes dissociate more as concentration decreases (dilution), producing more ions per mole and hence sharply higher molar conductivity, approaching $\Lambda_m^\circ$ only at infinite dilution.
questions.trick: Weak electrolyte: dilution boosts dissociation → $\Lambda_m$ shoots up.

questions.q: Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions is used to determine
options: the rate constant of a reaction
$\Lambda_m^\circ$ of a weak electrolyte from $\Lambda_m^\circ$ values of strong electrolytes
questions.explanation: Since weak electrolytes cannot be extrapolated directly to infinite dilution, $\Lambda_m^\circ$ for e.g. CH$_3$COOH is obtained as $\Lambda_m^\circ(CH_3COONa) + \Lambda_m^\circ(HCl) - \Lambda_m^\circ(NaCl)$, using Kohlrausch's law that each ion contributes independently.
questions.trick: Kohlrausch's law builds weak electrolyte $\Lambda_m^\circ$ from strong-electrolyte data.

questions.q: If $E^\circ_{cell} = 0.0591$ V and n = 1 for a cell at 298 K, the equilibrium constant $K_c$ of the reaction is
questions.explanation: $\log K_c = \dfrac{nE^\circ_{cell}}{0.0591} = \dfrac{1\times0.0591}{0.0591} = 1 \Rightarrow K_c = 10$.
questions.trick: $\log K_c=\dfrac{nE^\circ_{cell}}{0.0591}$ — Nernst-derived shortcut.

questions.q: For the cell reaction M(s) + N$^{2+}$(aq, 0.001 M) $\to$ M$^{2+}$(aq, 0.1 M) + N(s), with $E^\circ_{cell} = 0.30$ V, n = 2, the EMF at 298 K is (use $\dfrac{0.0591}{2}\log(100) = 0.0591$)
questions.trick: Nernst: $E_{cell}=E^\circ-\dfrac{0.0591}{n}\log Q$, Q = products/reactants conc.

questions.q: In a lead storage battery during discharge, the electrode reactions convert PbO$_2$ and Pb into
questions.explanation: During discharge, Pb (anode) is oxidised to PbSO$_4$ and PbO$_2$ (cathode) is reduced to PbSO$_4$, consuming H$_2$SO$_4$ from the electrolyte.
questions.trick: Lead-acid discharge: both Pb and PbO$_2$ end up as PbSO$_4$.

questions.q: The H$_2$-O$_2$ fuel cell is considered pollution-free mainly because
options: it does not require an electrolyte
it operates without any current flow
the only product formed is water
questions.explanation: In a H$_2$-O$_2$ fuel cell, hydrogen is oxidised at the anode and oxygen reduced at the cathode (with KOH electrolyte), giving water as the sole product, so no pollutants are released.
questions.trick: H$_2$-O$_2$ fuel cell's only product is water — zero pollution.

questions.q: Rusting of iron is best described as
options: a process that requires no moisture
an electrochemical process involving oxidation of Fe at anodic sites and reduction of O$_2$ at cathodic sites
a purely chemical reaction with no electron transfer
a physical adsorption of oxygen on iron
questions.explanation: Rusting is electrochemical corrosion: Fe is oxidised (Fe $\to$ Fe$^{2+}$ + 2e$^-$) at anodic spots, and O$_2$ is reduced at cathodic spots (with moisture as the medium), ultimately forming hydrated Fe$_2$O$_3$.
questions.trick: Rusting = electrochemical: Fe oxidised at anode spot, O$_2$ reduced at cathode spot.

questions.q: Sacrificial protection of iron pipelines uses blocks of
options: copper, since it is more noble than iron
gold, since it does not corrode
zinc or magnesium, since they are more reactive than iron
lead, since it is denser than iron
questions.explanation: A more reactive metal like Zn or Mg is connected to iron; it oxidises preferentially (acts as the anode), protecting the iron (cathode) from corrosion.
questions.trick: Sacrificial anode must be MORE reactive than iron (Zn/Mg).

questions.q: For a strong electrolyte, molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ varies with $\sqrt{C}$ according to the Debye-Hückel-Onsager equation as
questions.explanation: For strong electrolytes, $\Lambda_m$ decreases slightly with increasing concentration due to inter-ionic attractions, following $\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A\sqrt{C}$; a plot of $\Lambda_m$ vs $\sqrt{C}$ is linear allowing extrapolation to get $\Lambda_m^\circ$.
questions.trick: Strong electrolyte: $\Lambda_m=\Lambda_m^\circ-A\sqrt{C}$, linear in $\sqrt{C}$.

questions.q: A solution of CuSO$_4$ is electrolysed for 10 minutes with a current of 1.5 A. The number of moles of electrons passed is (F = 96500 C mol$^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: Charge $= it = 1.5\times600 = 900$ C. Moles of electrons $= 900/96500 = 0.00933$ mol.
questions.trick: moles e⁻ $=\dfrac{it}{F}$ — charge over Faraday constant.

questions.q: In an electrolytic cell (unlike a galvanic cell), the anode is
questions.explanation: In electrolysis, the anode is connected to the positive terminal of the external battery and oxidation still occurs there — only the polarity convention differs from a galvanic cell (where the anode is negative).
questions.trick: Electrolytic cell: anode is still oxidation but wired to +ve terminal.

questions.q: Given $E^\circ_{Ag^+/Ag} = 0.80$ V and $E^\circ_{Zn^{2+}/Zn} = -0.76$ V, which statement about the cell Zn|Zn$^{2+}$||Ag$^+$|Ag is correct?
options: The cell reaction is non-spontaneous since $E^\circ_{cell} < 0$
$E^\circ_{cell} = 1.56$ V and the reaction is spontaneous
Silver is oxidised in this cell
questions.explanation: $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode} = 0.80 - (-0.76) = 1.56$ V $> 0$, so the reaction Zn + 2Ag$^+$ $\to$ Zn$^{2+}$ + 2Ag is spontaneous.
questions.trick: Higher $E^\circ$ = cathode; $E^\circ_{cell}=E_{cathode}-E_{anode}>0$ means spontaneous.

questions.q: The conductivity of a 0.01 M solution is $1.5\times10^{-3}$ S cm$^{-1}$. Its molar conductivity is
questions.explanation: $\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa\times1000}{C} = \dfrac{1.5\times10^{-3}\times1000}{0.01} = 150$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: $\Lambda_m=\dfrac{\kappa\times1000}{C}$ — molar conductivity from conductivity and molarity.

questions.q: Which of the following is a primary cell (non-rechargeable)?
questions.explanation: The Leclanché (dry) cell is a primary cell — once its reactants are consumed it cannot be recharged, unlike lead storage, Ni-Cd or Li-ion cells which are secondary (rechargeable).
questions.trick: Primary cell = one-use, cannot recharge (Leclanché/dry cell).

questions.q: For the standard hydrogen electrode to have $E^\circ = 0.00$ V, the conditions required are
options: 1 M H$^+$, 1 bar H$_2$ gas, 298 K, Pt electrode
pure water with a Pt electrode
1 M H$^+$ only, gas pressure irrelevant
any concentration of H$^+$ at 273 K
questions.explanation: By convention, the SHE is assigned $E^\circ = 0$ V under standard conditions: 1 M H$^+$ ion concentration, H$_2$ gas at 1 bar pressure, 298 K, using an inert Pt electrode.
questions.trick: SHE reference: 1 M H$^+$, 1 bar H$_2$, 298 K, Pt, by definition $E^\circ=0$.

questions.q: The cell constant of a conductivity cell is defined as
options: the product of conductivity and molarity
the ratio of resistance to conductance
the ratio of the distance between the electrodes (l) to the area of cross-section (A)
questions.explanation: Cell constant $G^* = l/A$ is a fixed geometric property of the conductivity cell, used to convert measured conductance into conductivity: $\kappa = G^*\times G$ (G = measured conductance).
questions.trick: Cell constant $G^*=l/A$ — pure geometry of the conductivity cell.

questions.q: A conductivity cell with cell constant 1.5 cm$^{-1}$ shows a measured conductance of $2\times10^{-3}$ S for an electrolyte solution. The conductivity of the solution is
questions.explanation: $\kappa = G^*\times G = 1.5\times2\times10^{-3} = 3\times10^{-3}$ S cm$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: $\kappa=G^*\times G$ — cell constant times measured conductance.

questions.q: For an electrolyte that furnishes $z$ charges per formula unit (e.g. $z=2$ for CuSO$_4$), the equivalent conductivity $\Lambda_{eq}$ is related to the molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ by
questions.explanation: Equivalent conductivity is molar conductivity divided by the number of charges (equivalents) furnished per formula unit, $\Lambda_{eq} = \Lambda_m/z$.
questions.trick: $\Lambda_{eq}=\Lambda_m/z$ — divide by charge number per formula unit.

questions.q: For the concentration cell Cu(s)|Cu$^{2+}$(0.01 M)||Cu$^{2+}$(1 M)|Cu(s) at 298 K (n = 2), the EMF of the cell is
questions.explanation: For a concentration cell, $E^\circ_{cell}=0$, and $E_{cell} = \dfrac{0.0591}{2}\log\dfrac{[Cu^{2+}]_{cathode}}{[Cu^{2+}]_{anode}} = \dfrac{0.0591}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{0.01} = \dfrac{0.0591}{2}\times2 = 0.0591$ V.
questions.trick: Concentration cell: $E_{cell}=\dfrac{0.0591}{n}\log\dfrac{C_{cathode}}{C_{anode}}$, $E^\circ=0$.

questions.q: The salt bridge in a galvanic cell mainly functions to
options: supply electrons to the external circuit
maintain electrical neutrality in each half-cell by allowing ion flow, completing the internal circuit
increase the EMF of the cell
act as the site of oxidation
questions.explanation: As the cell reaction proceeds, charge builds up in each half-cell; the salt bridge allows ions to migrate between the half-cells to maintain electrical neutrality and complete the circuit, while minimising the liquid-junction potential.
questions.trick: Salt bridge = ion flow to keep both half-cells electrically neutral.

questions.q: Among common elements, fluorine (F$_2$/F$^-$) has the highest standard reduction potential, making it
options: the strongest oxidising agent among common species
questions.explanation: A high (very positive) standard reduction potential means the species is easily reduced, i.e. it is a strong oxidising agent; F$_2$ has the highest $E^\circ$ in the electrochemical series.
questions.trick: Most positive $E^\circ_{red}$ = easiest to reduce = strongest oxidiser (F$_2$).

questions.q: Given $E^\circ_{Ag^+/Ag} = 0.80$ V and $E^\circ_{Cu^{2+}/Cu} = 0.34$ V, which of the following is TRUE?
options: Neither metal can displace the other's ion
Ag metal can displace Cu$^{2+}$ from CuSO$_4$ solution
Both metals have identical reducing power
Cu metal can displace Ag$^+$ from AgNO$_3$ solution, since Cu is the better reducing agent
questions.explanation: A metal with a lower (more negative/less positive) standard reduction potential is the better reducing agent and will displace a metal ion with higher $E^\circ$ from solution; since $E^\circ_{Cu}< E^\circ_{Ag}$, Cu displaces Ag$^+$ from solution.
questions.trick: Lower $E^\circ$ metal is the better reducing agent, displaces the higher one.

questions.q: The quantity of electricity required to deposit 1 mole of aluminium metal from molten Al$_2$O$_3$ (Al$^{3+}$ + 3e$^-$ $\to$ Al) is
questions.explanation: Since 3 electrons are needed per Al$^{3+}$ ion, 1 mole of Al requires 3 Faradays of charge $= 3\times96500 = 289500$ C.
questions.trick: Charge needed = n (electrons per ion) $\times$ 96500 C per mole.

questions.q: In electroplating an object with a metal such as silver or chromium, the object to be plated is made the
questions.explanation: In electroplating (an electrolytic process), the object to be plated is connected as the cathode so that metal cations from the electrolyte are reduced and deposited onto its surface.
questions.trick: Electroplating: object to be plated = cathode (gets reduced metal).

questions.q: Hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells are generally more efficient at converting chemical energy to useful work than conventional combustion (heat) engines because
options: fuel cells operate at very high temperatures
fuel cells convert chemical energy directly to electrical energy, avoiding the intermediate heat-to-work conversion limited by Carnot efficiency
fuel cells do not use catalysts
questions.explanation: Combustion engines first convert chemical energy to heat, then heat to work, and are limited by Carnot (thermodynamic) efficiency; fuel cells convert chemical energy directly to electrical energy, bypassing this limitation and achieving higher efficiency.
questions.trick: Fuel cells skip Carnot-limited heat→work step, going chemical→electrical directly.

questions.q: Unlike metallic conductors, the conductivity of an electrolytic solution generally
options: increases with increase in temperature, due to increased ionic mobility and degree of dissociation
questions.explanation: Raising the temperature decreases the viscosity of the solvent (increasing ionic mobility) and increases the degree of dissociation of weak electrolytes, so electrolytic conductivity rises with temperature — opposite to metals, where conductivity falls.
questions.trick: Electrolytes: heat → more dissociation + mobility → conductivity UP (opposite of metals).

questions.q: In the chlor-alkali process (electrolysis of concentrated aqueous NaCl), the products formed are
options: Na metal at the cathode and Cl$_2$ at the anode
only NaOH, with no gaseous products
H$_2$ at the cathode, Cl$_2$ at the anode, and NaOH remains in solution
questions.explanation: Water is preferentially reduced at the cathode (giving H$_2$ and OH$^-$) rather than Na$^+$ (which has a much more negative reduction potential), while Cl$^-$ is oxidised at the anode to Cl$_2$; NaOH accumulates in the solution.
questions.trick: Chlor-alkali: water reduced (H$_2$) at cathode beats Na$^+$; Cl$^-$ oxidised at anode.

questions.q: For a cell with n = 2 and $E^\circ_{cell} = 0.295$ V at 298 K, the equilibrium constant $K_c$ of the cell reaction is approximately
questions.explanation: $\log K_c = \dfrac{nE^\circ_{cell}}{0.0591} = \dfrac{2\times0.295}{0.0591} = \dfrac{0.59}{0.0591}\approx10$, so $K_c \approx 10^{10}$.
questions.trick: $\log K_c=\dfrac{nE^\circ}{0.0591}$; compute exponent then $K_c=10^{\text{exponent}}$.

questions.q: The SI-compatible unit commonly used to express the specific conductance (conductivity) of an electrolytic solution is
questions.explanation: Conductivity $\kappa$ is the reciprocal of resistivity and is expressed in siemens per centimetre (S cm$^{-1}$) or siemens per metre (S m$^{-1}$).
questions.trick: Conductivity's SI-friendly unit: S cm$^{-1}$ (or S m$^{-1}$).

questions.q: A current of 2 A is passed through a CuSO$_4$ solution. The time (in seconds) required to deposit 6.35 g of Cu (M = 63.5, n = 2, F = 96500 C) is
questions.explanation: Moles of Cu $= 6.35/63.5 = 0.1$; charge needed $= 0.1\times2\times96500 = 19300$ C. Time $= Q/i = 19300/2 = 9650$ s.
questions.trick: $t=\dfrac{nFw}{Mi}$ — rearrange Faraday's law for time.

questions.q: Which statement about the Daniell cell, Zn(s)|Zn$^{2+}$(aq)||Cu$^{2+}$(aq)|Cu(s), is INCORRECT?
options: Electrons flow through the external circuit from the zinc electrode to the copper electrode
The copper electrode acts as the anode, where oxidation occurs
The concentration of Cu$^{2+}$ ions decreases as the cell operates
The mass of the zinc electrode decreases as the cell operates
questions.explanation: In the Daniell cell, copper is the cathode (site of reduction, Cu$^{2+}$ + 2e$^-$ $\to$ Cu); zinc is the anode (site of oxidation), so calling copper the anode is incorrect.
questions.trick: In Daniell cell Cu is always cathode (reduction), never anode.

questions.q: The electrochemical equivalent (Z) of a substance is related to its molar mass (M) and the number of electrons transferred (n) by
questions.explanation: By Faraday's first law, $w = Zit$, and since $w = \dfrac{Mit}{nF}$, comparing the two gives $Z = \dfrac{M}{nF}$, the mass deposited per coulomb of charge passed.
questions.trick: $Z=M/(nF)$ — electrochemical equivalent, mass per coulomb.

questions.q: Given $E^\circ_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}} = 0.77$ V and $E^\circ_{I_2/I^-} = 0.54$ V, the cell reaction $2Fe^{3+} + 2I^- \to 2Fe^{2+} + I_2$ has
questions.explanation: Fe$^{3+}$ is reduced (cathode) and I$^-$ is oxidised (anode): $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode}-E^\circ_{anode} = 0.77-0.54 = 0.23$ V $>0$, so the reaction is spontaneous, consistent with iodide reducing Fe$^{3+}$.
questions.trick: Higher $E^\circ$ species gets reduced (cathode); subtract to get $E^\circ_{cell}$.

questions.q: During the electrolysis of acidified water, 5.6 L of O$_2$ gas (at STP) is collected at the anode ($2H_2O \to O_2 + 4H^+ + 4e^-$). The charge passed is
questions.explanation: Moles of O$_2$ $= 5.6/22.4 = 0.25$ mol, requiring $0.25\times4 = 1$ mol electrons $= 1\times96500 = 96500$ C.
questions.trick: moles gas at anode $\times$ electrons per reaction $\times$ F = charge.

questions.q: For a redox couple with a very negative standard reduction potential (e.g. Li$^+$/Li, $E^\circ = -3.04$ V), the metal is
options: a very strong reducing agent, readily oxidised to its cation
a very poor reducing agent, difficult to oxidise
questions.explanation: A very negative reduction potential means the reverse (oxidation) reaction is highly favoured, so the metal readily loses electrons and acts as a strong reducing agent — Li is in fact the strongest reducing agent among common metals in aqueous solution.
questions.trick: Very negative $E^\circ_{red}$ → metal loses e⁻ easily → strong reducing agent.
